subskill: Range of a fee giving an exact count of visit numbers
prompt: A climbing gym offers two plans. Plan A has a one-time fee of k dollars plus $12 per visit. Plan B has a one-time fee of 3k dollars plus $5 per visit. Dana will make n visits, where n is a positive whole number. She wants Plan A to cost less than Plan B, and she wants Plan A to cost at most $260 in total. For some integer values of k, exactly 6 values of n meet both of Dana's conditions. What is the difference between the greatest and least such values of k?
explanation: Plan A costs less than Plan B when k + 12n < 3k + 5n, that is, 7n < 2k, or n < 2k/7. Plan A costs at most $260 when k + 12n ≤ 260, that is, n ≤ (260 - k)/12. The first bound rises as k rises and the second falls, so the number of qualifying n is set by whichever bound is smaller. For small k the first bound decides: exactly 6 positive n are below 2k/7 when 6 < 2k/7 ≤ 7, so 21 < k ≤ 24.5, giving k = 22, 23, 24 (at k = 21, 2k/7 = 6 exactly and n = 6 does not satisfy the strict 'less than', so only 5 values work); for these k the budget bound is far above 6. For large k the budget decides: exactly 6 positive n are at most (260 - k)/12 when 6 ≤ (260 - k)/12 < 7, so 176 < k ≤ 188, giving k = 177 through 188 (at k = 188 the bound is exactly 6, and n = 6 is allowed because the budget is 'at most'); for these k the first bound is far above 6. For k between 25 and 176 both bounds allow more than 6 values. The greatest k is 188 and the least is 22, so the difference is 188 - 22 = 166. Choice 167 comes from treating 'less than' as 'no more than', which lets k = 21 in. Choice 182 comes from counting n = 0 as a possible number of visits, which moves the least k to 18 and the greatest to 200. Choice 136 comes from adding the per-visit prices instead of subtracting them, 17n < 2k, which moves the least k to 52.
mechanism: two linear bounds on n, one rising and one falling in k
the smaller bound sets the count
strict 'less than' at k = 21 and attained 'at most' at k = 188
greatest minus least k across two separate blocks
quantity_asked: the greatest integer k minus the least integer k for which exactly 6 positive whole numbers n satisfy both conditions

setup.i: k is the one-time fee of one plan and 3k the fee of another, so the number of whole-number visit counts is capped by the smaller of a bound that rises with k (the cheaper-plan condition) and one that falls with k (the budget)
setup.ii: exactly 6 positive whole numbers of visits meet both conditions
